claim: Mitochondrial gene sequences diverge at 10–30 times the mean rate of nuclear genes in mammals.
source: In mammals, mitochondrial gene sequences diverge at 10–30 times the mean rate of nuclear genes (Lynch et al., 2006; Allio et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lynch et al., 2006 and Allio et al., 2017

claim: The faster divergence rate of mitochondrial genes is typically ascribed to a faster underlying mutation rate and limited scope for purifying selection.
source: This difference is typically ascribed to a faster underlying mutation rate and limited scope for purifying selection on mitochondrial genes, given uniparental inheritance, negligible recombination, and high ploidy (Rand, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rand, 2001

claim: The prevalence of mitochondrial mutations in human populations is approximately 1 in 200.
source: At face value, weak selection against mitochondrial mutations might seem to be consistent with the high prevalence of mitochondrial mutations (~1 in 200) (Elliott et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Elliott et al., 2008

claim: The prevalence of mitochondrial diseases in human populations is approximately 1 in 5000 births.
source: and diseases (~1 in 5000 births) (Schaefer et al., 2008) in human populations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schaefer et al., 2008

claim: There is a strong signal of purifying selection on mitochondrial genes.
source: But it is not consistent with the strong signal of purifying selection (da Fonseca et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to da Fonseca et al., 2008

claim: There is evidence of adaptive change in mitochondrial genes.
source: evidence of adaptive change (James et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to James et al., 2016

claim: Mitochondrial genes show codon bias.
source: and codon bias (Yang and Nielsen, 2008) in mitochondrial genes
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang and Nielsen, 2008

claim: There is a low transmission rate of severe mitochondrial mutations between generations.
source: nor with the low transmission rate of severe mitochondrial mutations between generations (Stewart et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stewart et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2014

claim: Female germline processes facilitate selection against mitochondrial mutations.
source: Despite the high rate of sequence divergence, female germline processes apparently facilitate selection against mitochondrial mutations, but the mechanisms are disputed and poorly understood (Burr et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burr et al., 2018

claim: The computational model incorporates de novo mitochondrial mutations and their segregation over multiple rounds of germ-cell division.
source: Our approach incorporates important factors neglected in earlier work, in particular the input of de novo mitochondrial mutations and their segregation over multiple rounds of germ-cell division.
evidence: Description of the model approach in the manuscript

claim: The idea that mitochondrial mutations are winnowed through a tight germline bottleneck is pervasive in the literature.
source: The idea that mitochondrial mutations are winnowed through a tight germline bottleneck is pervasive in the literature and has long been held to explain sharp changes in mutation load between generations (Johnston et al., 2015; Floros et al., 2018; Stewart and Chinnery, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Johnston et al., 2015; Floros et al., 2018; Stewart and Chinnery, 2015

claim: Estimates of the exact size of the mitochondrial bottleneck span two orders of magnitude.
source: The exact size of the bottleneck is unclear, with estimates from mouse (Wai et al., 2008; Cree et al., 2008; Cao et al., 2009) and human studies (Floros et al., 2018; Rebolledo-Jaramillo et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2013; Li et al., 2016) spanning two orders of magnitude.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Tighter bottlenecks produce greater variance in mutation loads among resulting germ cells.
source: Bottlenecks generate variance in mutation loads among the resulting germ cells, and tighter bottlenecks produce greater variance, offering scope for selection against mitochondrial mutations at the level of the individual (Bergstrom and Pritchard, 1998; Roze et al., 2005; Hadjivasiliou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bergstrom and Pritchard, 1998; Roze et al., 2005; Hadjivasiliou et al., 2013

claim: Bottlenecks induce greater input of de novo mutations as more rounds of mitochondrial replication are required to regenerate extreme ploidy.
source: Second, bottlenecks induce greater input of de novo mutations as more rounds of mitochondrial replication are required to regenerate the extreme ploidy of mitochondrial DNA in mature oocytes.
evidence: Logical inference from the model structure

claim: In humans, the number of germ cells declines dramatically in the foetus between mid-gestation when there are 7–8 million oocytes.
source: In humans (Albamonte et al., 2008; Kaipia and Hsueh, 1997), the number of germ cells declines dramatically in the foetus between mid-gestation (~20 weeks in humans) when there are 7–8 million oocytes
evidence: Supported by citations to Albamonte et al., 2008; Kaipia and Hsueh, 1997

claim: At least two thirds of oocytes are lost by late gestation, leaving a reserve of 1–2 million at birth.
source: to late gestation when at least two thirds of these are lost, leaving a reserve of 1–2 million at birth (Townson and Combelles, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Townson and Combelles, 2012

claim: Oocyte loss continues throughout the life of an individual, eventually leading to menopause.
source: Oocyte loss continues throughout the life of an individual, eventually leading to the depletion of the ovarian pool and loss of reproductive function at menopause (Suganuma et al., 1993; Galimov et al., 2014; Cummins, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Suganuma et al., 1993; Galimov et al., 2014; Cummins, 2004

claim: Similar loss of female germ cells before sexual maturity is evident in mice and several other animal species.
source: Similar loss of female germ cells before sexual maturity is evident in mice and several other animal species (Nezis et al., 2000; Rodrigues et al., 2009; Saidapur, 1978; Morita and Tilly, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nezis et al., 2000; Rodrigues et al., 2009; Saidapur, 1978; Morita and Tilly, 1999

claim: Germ cell attrition has historically been ascribed to cell death during oocyte maturation.
source: This attrition has historically been ascribed to cell death during oocyte maturation (Tilly, 2001; Perez et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to Tilly, 2001; Perez et al., 2000

claim: More recent findings implicate the apoptotic loss of 'nurse cells' during the genesis of primary oocytes.
source: but more recent findings implicate the apoptotic loss of 'nurse cells' during the genesis of primary oocytes (Lei and Spradling, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lei and Spradling, 2016

claim: The Balbiani body is a prominent feature of the human and mouse female germline.
source: A more recent interpretation of germ-cell loss links it to the formation of the Balbiani body, a prominent feature of the human (Motta et al., 2000; Hertig, 1968) and mouse (Lei and Spradling, 2016; Kloc et al., 2004) female germline
evidence: Supported by citations to Motta et al., 2000; Hertig, 1968; Lei and Spradling, 2016; Kloc et al., 2004

claim: In the mouse, proliferating germ cells typically form clusters of five to eight cells that establish cytoplasmic bridges.
source: In the mouse, proliferating germ cells typically form clusters of five to eight cells that establish cytoplasmic bridges (Lei and Spradling, 2016; Pepling et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lei and Spradling, 2016; Pepling et al., 2007

claim: Around half the mitochondria from each nurse cell are streamed into the Balbiani body of the primary oocyte.
source: It is thought that around half the mitochondria from each nurse cell are streamed into the Balbiani body of the primary oocyte, through an active cytoskeletal process that seems to depend in part on the membrane potential of discrete mitochondria (Zhou et al., 2010; Bilinski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2010; Bilinski et al., 2017

claim: Nurse cells undergo apoptosis after mitochondrial transfer to the Balbiani body.
source: The remaining nurse cells, now denuded of half their mitochondria, undergo apoptosis (Lei and Spradling, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lei and Spradling, 2016

claim: Selection at the organelle level through the pooling of high-quality mitochondria into the Balbiani body is a more potent force than germline bottlenecks and follicular atresia.
source: Our results show that selection at the organelle level through the pooling of high-quality mitochondria into the Balbiani body is a more potent force than germline bottlenecks and follicular atresia and must play a key role in the maintenance of mitochondrial function in the face of pervasive mutational pressure.
evidence: Based on computational and evolutionary modeling results presented in the manuscript

claim: The zygote is assumed to have around half a million copies of mitochondrial DNA (exact number 2^19).
source: The zygote is assumed to have around half a million copies of mitochondrial DNA (exact number 219)
evidence: Model parameter specification

claim: The pattern of segregation is in agreement with recent evidence for actin-mediated mixing of mitochondria within cells during mitosis leading to random segregation.
source: The pattern of segregation is in agreement with recent evidence for actin-mediated mixing of mitochondria within cells during mitosis leading to random segregation (Moore et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore et al., 2021

claim: Mitochondrial networks fragment into multiple smaller structures at cell division that probably contain one or a few mtDNAs.
source: This assumption is supported by evidence that mitochondrial networks fragment into multiple smaller structures at cell division (Taguchi et al., 2007; Park and Cho, 2012) that probably contain one or a few mtDNAs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Taguchi et al., 2007; Park and Cho, 2012

claim: Mitochondrial replication is not active during early embryo development.
source: Mitochondrial replication is not active during early embryo development (Dumollard et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumollard et al., 2007

claim: After 12 cell divisions, a random group of 32 cells form the primordial germ cells (PGC) in humans.
source: In humans, after 12 cell divisions a random group of 32 cells form the primordial germ cells (PGC) (Extavour and Akam, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Extavour and Akam, 2003

claim: Mitochondrial replication resumes at the point of PGC specification.
source: Mitochondrial replication resumes at this point (Albamonte et al., 2008; Dumollard et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albamonte et al., 2008; Dumollard et al., 2007

claim: Point mutations during replication are the dominant form of mutation in mtDNA.
source: Point mutations during replication are the dominant form of mutation in mtDNA, so we do not consider damage from other sources such as oxidative damage (Stewart and Larsson, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stewart and Larsson, 2014

claim: Mitotic proliferation of PGCs gives rise to ~8 million oogonia, which are reduced to ~1 million primary oocytes during late gestation.
source: Mitotic proliferation of PGCs gives rise to ~8 million oogonia, which are reduced to ~1 million primary oocytes during late gestation (Figure 1B; Albamonte et al., 2008; Dumollard et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albamonte et al., 2008; Dumollard et al., 2007 and shown in Figure 1B

claim: Mutations accumulate far more slowly during the quiescent phase of primary oocytes.
source: Mutations accumulate far more slowly during this phase, which persists over decades in humans (Dumollard et al., 2007; Allen and de Paula, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dumollard et al., 2007; Allen and de Paula, 2013

claim: At puberty, the primary oocytes mature through clonal amplification of mitochondria back to extreme ploidy (~500,000 copies) in mature oocytes.
source: At puberty, the primary oocytes mature through clonal amplification of mitochondria back to the extreme ploidy in mature oocytes (~500,000 copies; Figure 1B; Radzvilavicius et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radzvilavicius et al., 2016 and shown in Figure 1B

claim: Tighter bottlenecks at early developmental stage generate greater segregational variance in mutation load between cells.
source: Tighter bottlenecks at this early developmental stage generate greater segregational variance in mutation load between cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B from computational model results

claim: Bottlenecks create the possibility that cells can be mutation free even when initiated from a zygote that contains significant numbers of mutations.
source: The bottleneck not only creates a wider spread of mutation number per cell, but also the possibility that cells can be mutation free even when initiated from a zygote that contains significant numbers of mutations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2B from computational model results

claim: Bottlenecks in themselves do not change the mean mutation load.
source: Bottlenecks in themselves do not change the mean mutation load, as they occur before the start of mitochondrial replication (i.e. at PGC specification; Figure 2B; Dumollard et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumollard et al., 2007 and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Individual fitness is defined by a concave fitness function based on the observed dependence of mitochondrial diseases on mutation load.
source: Based on the observed dependence of mitochondrial diseases on mutation load (Rossignol et al., 2003; Kopinski et al., 2019; Wallace and Chalkia, 2013), in which more serious phenotypes typically manifest only at high mutation loads of >60 % (Rossignol et al., 2003; Kopinski et al., 2019; Wallace and Chalkia, 2013), it is thought that individual fitness is defined by a concave fitness function, indicative of negative epistasis (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossignol et al., 2003; Kopinski et al., 2019; Wallace and Chalkia, 2013 and shown in Figure 2C

claim: Tight bottlenecks are advantageous only for rare individuals who inherit high mutation loads.
source: In sum: even though bottlenecks generate greater variance, they impose the need for additional rounds of mitochondrial replication during oocyte maturation, resulting in greater de novo mutational input. This makes tight bottlenecks advantageous only for rare individuals who inherit high mutation loads, but not for the great majority of the population where the prevalence of mitochondrial mutations is below the limits of detectability, between 0.001 and 0.01 (Elliott et al., 2008; Floros et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on computational model results and supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2008; Floros et al., 2018

claim: The loss of ~80% of oocytes via follicular atresia during late gestation has long been puzzling.
source: However, the loss of ~80% of oocytes via follicular atresia during late gestation has long been puzzling and could arguably reflect selection against cells with higher mutation loads.
evidence: General statement about the field

claim: Pooling of mitochondria into the Balbiani body increases the number of mitochondria in primary oocytes.
source: The first benefit of mitochondrial transfer into the Balbiani body is that pooling increases the number of mitochondria in primary oocytes.
evidence: Based on computational model results

claim: Pooling cuts the number of rounds of replication needed to reach extreme ploidy in mature oocytes, which decreases the input of new mutations.
source: Pooling therefore cuts the number of rounds of replication needed to reach the extreme ploidy required by mature oocytes, which decreases the input of new mutations from replication errors during oocyte maturation.
evidence: Logical inference from the model structure

claim: Nurse cells retain a higher fraction of mutant mitochondria but undergo apoptosis, removing mutants from the pool of germ cells.
source: Nurse cells retain a higher fraction of mutant mitochondria but undergo apoptosis, removing mutants from the pool of germ cells, and explaining the need for an extreme loss of germ cells during late gestation.
evidence: Based on computational model results

claim: The evolutionary model evaluates long-term evolutionary change in an infinite population with non-overlapping generations.
source: This evolutionary model evaluates long-term evolutionary change in an infinite population with non-overlapping generations and is implemented using a number of approximations, which greatly reduce the model complexity (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Description of the evolutionary model approach

claim: 99.5% of individuals are 'mutation free' (carry <2% mutants) in human populations.
source: Specifically, we used estimated values of 1/5000 for mitochondrial disease (>60% mutant), 1/200 for carriers of mitochondrial mutants (2–60% mutant) and hence 99.5% of individuals are 'mutation free' (i.e. carry <2% mutants, the threshold for detection in these estimates of mutation frequency [Elliott et al., 2008; Schaefer et al., 2008]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2008; Schaefer et al., 2008

claim: A minor allele frequency of 1–2% is relatively common in selected human PGCs based on deep-sequencing estimates.
source: Recent deep-sequencing estimates using a mutation detection threshold of >1% (Floros et al., 2018), show that a minor allele frequency of 1–2% is relatively common in selected human PGCs
evidence: Supported by citation to Floros et al., 2018

claim: Selection at the level of individuals or cells alone do not readily approximate the clinical data whatever the bottleneck size.
source: Likelihood heatmaps confirm that selection at the level of individuals or cells alone do not readily approximate the clinical data whatever the bottleneck size (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A-B from evolutionary model results

claim: Mitochondrial DNA accumulates mutations faster than nuclear genes.
source: At the heart of this problem is the paradox that mtDNA accumulates mutations faster than nuclear genes, yet there is evidence that mtDNA is under strong purifying selection.
evidence: General statement supported by earlier citations in the manuscript

claim: Mitochondrial mutations accumulate through Muller's ratchet, as mtDNA is exclusively maternally inherited and does not undergo recombination through meiosis.
source: Mitochondrial mutations accumulate through Muller's ratchet, as mtDNA is exclusively maternally inherited, and does not undergo recombination through meiosis (Rand, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rand, 2001

claim: Mitochondrial genes are highly polyploid, which obscures the relationship between genotype and phenotype.
source: In addition, mitochondrial genes are highly polyploid, which obscures the relationship between genotype and phenotype, hindering the effectiveness of selection on individuals.
evidence: General statement based on established knowledge

claim: Deleterious mitochondrial mutations seem to be eliminated effectively.
source: Despite these constraints, deleterious mitochondrial mutations seem to be eliminated effectively (da Fonseca et al., 2008; James et al., 2016; Yang and Nielsen, 2008; Stewart et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Most work to date has focused on the mitochondrial bottleneck as a means of generating variation in mitochondrial content between oocytes.
source: Most work to date (Johnston et al., 2015, Stewart and Chinnery, 2015; Wai et al., 2008; Cree et al., 2008; Cao et al., 2009) has focused on the mitochondrial bottleneck as a means of generating variation in mitochondrial content between oocytes and by extension zygotes (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Earlier work neglects the introduction of de novo mitochondrial mutations produced by copying errors.
source: More significantly, this earlier work neglects an important germline feature, the introduction of de novo mitochondrial mutations produced by copying errors (Arbeithuber et al., 2020) rather than damage by reactive oxygen species (Stewart and Larsson, 2014, Trifunovic et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arbeithuber et al., 2020; Stewart and Larsson, 2014; Trifunovic et al., 2005

claim: Tighter bottlenecks are disadvantageous as they impose the need for more rounds of mitochondrial replication which means a greater input of de novo mutations.
source: Tighter bottlenecks are disadvantageous as they impose the need for more rounds of mitochondrial replication which means a greater input of de novo mutations.
evidence: Based on computational model results

claim: Most individuals have low mutation loads (~99.5% in human populations).
source: Most individuals have low mutation loads (~99.5% in human populations [Elliott et al., 2008; Schaefer et al., 2008])
evidence: Supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2008; Schaefer et al., 2008

claim: For most individuals, the normal process of repeated segregation during cell division generates sufficient variance in itself.
source: and for them, the normal process of repeated segregation during cell division generates sufficient variance in itself.
evidence: Based on computational model results

claim: The reduction in mitochondrial copy numbers from zygote to primordial germ cells should be thought of as the reestablishment of a typical copy number at the start of cellular differentiation.
source: In fact, the reduction in mitochondrial copy numbers from zygote to primordial germ cells should be thought of as the reestablishment of a typical copy number at the start of cellular differentiation, which commences after multiple cell divisions without mtDNA replication.
evidence: Interpretation based on model results

claim: The extreme ploidy in the zygote allows early rounds of cell division to occur without mitochondrial replication, and hence without de novo mutational input.
source: The extreme ploidy in the zygote allows early rounds of cell division to occur without mitochondrial replication, and hence without de novo mutational input.
evidence: Logical inference from the model structure

claim: At the point of cellular differentiation, there is homogeneity in the mutation load among the different organ systems.
source: So at the point of cellular differentiation (~12 cell divisions), there is homogeneity in the mutation load among the different organ systems and no one system is likely to fail, which would massively lower the fitness of the whole organism (Radzvilavicius et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radzvilavicius et al., 2016

claim: Organisms with modular growth neither sequester a recognizable germline distinct from the stem-cell lineage early in development nor have oocytes with massively expanded mitochondrial numbers.
source: This contrasts with organisms that have modular growth, such as plants and morphologically simple metazoa (sponges, corals, placozoa), which neither sequester a recognizable germline distinct from the stem-cell lineage early in development (although recent work challenges this view, Lanfear, 2018), nor have oocytes with massively expanded mitochondrial numbers (Extavour and Akam, 2003; Radzvilavicius et al., 2016; Extavour, 2007; Blackstone and Jasker, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lanfear, 2018; Extavour and Akam, 2003; Radzvilavicius et al., 2016; Extavour, 2007; Blackstone and Jasker, 2003

claim: It is unlikely that such a high proportion of germ cells could have low fitness due to mitochondrial mutations.
source: It is unlikely to be random, yet does not obviously serve a selective function, as it seems unlikely that such a high proportion of germ cells could have low fitness (Krakauer and Mira, 1999; Chu et al., 2014; Haig, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krakauer and Mira, 1999; Chu et al., 2014; Haig, 2016

claim: Selection among PGCs at the end of the period of proliferation has little effect in significantly reducing mutation load.
source: The model confirms this intuition. Selection among PGCs at the end of the period of proliferation has little effect in significantly reducing mutation load (Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C from computational model results

claim: Cell-level selection produces little measurable reduction in mutation load and so is unlikely to be responsible for follicular atresia.
source: We conclude that cell-level selection produces little measurable reduction in mutation load and so is unlikely to be responsible for follicular atresia.
evidence: Based on computational model results

claim: In many metazoa, the over-proliferation of PGCs culminates in their organization into germline cysts of multiple oogonia connected by cytoplasmic bridges.
source: In many metazoa, including clams (Reunov et al., 2019), insects (Tworzydlo et al., 2016; Cox and Spradling, 2003), mice (Pepling et al., 2007) and probably humans (Kloc et al., 2004), the over-proliferation of PGCs culminates in their organization into germline cysts of multiple oogonia connected by cytoplasmic bridges (Lei and Spradling, 2016; Pepling et al., 2007; Cox and Spradling, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Cytoplasmic connections allow the transfer of mitochondria and other cytoplasmic constituents by active attachment to microtubules into what becomes the primary oocyte.
source: These connections are thought to allow the transfer of mitochondria and other cytoplasmic constituents by active attachment to microtubules, into what becomes the primary oocyte (Lei and Spradling, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lei and Spradling, 2016

claim: Nurse cell death accounts for a considerable fraction of the germ cell loss usually ascribed to follicular atresia.
source: The plethora of terms should not mask the key point that nurse cell death accounts for a considerable fraction of the germ cell loss usually ascribed to follicular atresia.
evidence: Interpretation based on literature review

claim: Selective mitochondrial transfer into the Balbiani body purges mutations and pools high-quality mitochondria in a single cell.
source: We modeled selective mitochondrial transfer into the Balbiani body, perhaps in part reflecting membrane potential (Tworzydlo et al., 2016; Bilinski et al., 2017). This achieves two complementary benefits: it purges mutations and pools high-quality mitochondria in a single cell.
evidence: Based on computational model results and supported by citations to Tworzydlo et al., 2016; Bilinski et al., 2017

claim: If the germline cyst is composed of eight cells that contribute half of their mitochondria to the Balbiani body, then the primary oocyte gains four times as many mitochondria which have passed through quality control.
source: If the germline cyst is composed of eight cells that contribute half of their mitochondria to the Balbiani body then the primary oocyte gains four times as many mitochondria which have passed through quality control.
evidence: Logical inference from the model structure

claim: Selective transfer and pooling lowers the mutation load across a wide range of mutation rates and inherited loads.
source: Selective transfer and pooling lowers the mutation load across a wide range of mutation rates and inherited loads (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures from computational model results

claim: This process differs from mitophagy, as it not only removes mutant mitochondria, but crucially also increases mitochondrial numbers.
source: This process differs from mitophagy, the main route used in somatic cells for maintaining mitochondrial quality (Twig et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2007), as it not only removes mutant mitochondria, but crucially also increases mitochondrial numbers, a key requirement for prospective gametes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Twig et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2007

claim: Active spindle-associated mitochondrial migration to the generative oocyte occurs in the formation of polar bodies during meiosis I of oogenesis.
source: The requirement for pooling of mitochondria to lower the mutation load from copying errors also aligns with experimental observations of active spindle-associated mitochondrial migration to the generative oocyte in the formation of polar bodies during meiosis I of oogenesis (Dalton and Carroll, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dalton and Carroll, 2013

claim: Selection for mitochondrial quality occurs during polar body formation (i.e. polar bodies retain mutant mitochondria).
source: We predict that selection for mitochondrial quality occurs during this process (i.e. polar bodies retain mutant mitochondria) but have not dealt with that explicitly in the model.
evidence: Prediction based on model results

claim: Strong selective pooling of mitochondria into the Balbiani body predicts the observed prevalence of mitochondrial mutations and diseases in human populations under a wide range of mutation rates and bottleneck sizes.
source: Strong selective pooling of mitochondria into the Balbiani body predicts the observed prevalence of mitochondrial mutations and diseases in human populations (Elliott et al., 2008; Schaefer et al., 2008) under a wide range of mutation rates and bottleneck sizes (Figure 5).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5 from evolutionary model results and supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2008; Schaefer et al., 2008

claim: Higher mutation rates (10^−7 per base pair) strengthen the conclusions about the importance of organelle-level selection.
source: In general, higher mutation rates (10−7 per base pair) strengthen the conclusions discussed here (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 from computational model results

claim: The lowest mutation rates are more commensurate with weaker forms of evolutionary constraint generated by selection on individuals or cells.
source: whereas the lowest mutation rates are more commensurate with weaker forms of evolutionary constraint generated by selection on individuals or cells.
evidence: Based on evolutionary model results

claim: Low mutation rates are not consistent with the 10-30-fold faster evolution rates of mtDNA compared with nuclear genes.
source: However, such low mutation rates are not consistent with the 10-30-fold faster evolution rates of mtDNA compared with nuclear genes (Lynch et al., 2006; Allio et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lynch et al., 2006; Allio et al., 2017

claim: Oxidative mutations may accumulate over female reproductive lifespans, perhaps contributing to the timing of the menopause.
source: While this source of mutation is likely low compared with copying errors (Stewart and Larsson, 2014; Arbeithuber et al., 2020), oxidative mutations may accumulate over female reproductive lifespans (Trifunovic et al., 2005), perhaps contributing to the timing of the menopause (Shoubridge and Wai, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stewart and Larsson, 2014; Arbeithuber et al., 2020; Trifunovic et al., 2005; Shoubridge and Wai, 2007

claim: Primary oocytes contain ~6000 mitochondria.
source: As primary oocytes contain ~6000 mitochondria (Shoubridge and Wai, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Shoubridge and Wai, 2007

claim: Expansion up to ~500,000 copies in the mature oocyte will amplify any mutations acquired during oocyte arrest at prophase I.
source: expansion up to ~500,000 copies in the mature oocyte will amplify any mutations acquired during oocyte arrest at prophase I, potentially over decades (Arbeithuber et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arbeithuber et al., 2020

claim: The metabolic quiescence of oocytes can best be understood in light of the need to repress mitochondrial mutation accumulation during the extended period before reproduction.
source: The metabolic quiescence of oocytes can best be understood in light of the need to repress mitochondrial mutation accumulation during the extended period before reproduction (Allen and de Paula, 2013; de Paula et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen and de Paula, 2013; de Paula et al., 2013

claim: Mitochondrial DNA has persisted and has been at the heart of eukaryotic cell function for over a billion years.
source: yet like the Empire, which endured for another millennium, mitochondrial DNA has persisted and has been at the heart of eukaryotic cell function for over a billion years (Lane, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lane, 2005

claim: Direct selection for mitochondrial function during transfer into the Balbiani body is the most likely explanation of the observed prevalence of mitochondrial mutations and diseases in human populations.
source: We have modeled segregation and selection of mitochondrial DNA at each stage of germline development, and shown that direct selection for mitochondrial function during transfer into the Balbiani body is the most likely explanation of the observed prevalence of mitochondrial mutations and diseases in human populations.
evidence: Based on computational and evolutionary model results

claim: The mitochondria-centric model explains why mature oocytes are crammed with mitochondria.
source: More remarkably, this mitochondria-centric model elucidates the complexities of the female germline. It explains why mature oocytes are crammed with mitochondria (Radzvilavicius et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Radzvilavicius et al., 2016

claim: Sperm mitochondria are typically destroyed, giving rise to two sexes.
source: whereas sperm mitochondria are typically destroyed, giving rise to two sexes (Radzvilavicius et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Radzvilavicius et al., 2017

claim: The need for mitochondrial quality extends to somatic cells, as mitochondria activity is crucial to cellular, tissue, and organ functioning in the adult organism.
source: The need for mitochondrial quality extends to somatic cells, as mitochondria activity is crucial to cellular, tissue, and organ functioning in the adult organism (Pereira et al., 2021; Carelli et al., 2015; Diot et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pereira et al., 2021; Carelli et al., 2015; Diot et al., 2016

claim: Complex multicellularity requires passage through a single-celled, haploid stage to constrain the emergence of lower-level, selfish genetic elements.
source: Most fundamentally, this perspective challenges the claim that complex multicellularity requires passage through a single-celled, haploid stage to constrain the emergence of lower-level, selfish genetic elements (Buss, 1987; Maynard Smith and Szathmáry, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buss, 1987; Maynard Smith and Szathmáry, 1995

claim: Nuclear gene quality in oocytes is maintained by sexual exchange and recombination.
source: This is true for nuclear genes in oocytes, whose quality is maintained by sexual exchange and recombination (Maynard Smith and Szathmáry, 1995)
evidence: Supported by citation to Maynard Smith and Szathmáry, 1995

claim: Mitochondria are generally transmitted uniparentally, without sexual exchange or recombination.
source: but is not the case for mitochondria, which are generally transmitted uniparentally, without sexual exchange or recombination.
evidence: General statement based on established knowledge

claim: In animals, the oocyte cytoplasm is not derived from a single cell, but instead requires the selective pooling of mitochondrial DNA from clusters of progenitor cells.
source: In animals, the oocyte cytoplasm is not derived from a single cell, but instead requires the selective pooling of mitochondrial DNA from clusters of progenitor cells, which together generate high-quality mitochondria at extreme ploidy in mature gametes.
